forecasts-inflated-to-sell-loans.title_asserts: Lenders' project and programme forecasts are pushed upward on purpose so that countries take bigger loans.
forecasts-inflated-to-sell-loans.why: That programme growth forecasts are systematically too optimistic is established by the IMF's own evaluation office, which also says negotiation politics motivated ambitious projections. That is a finding about optimism and about pressure inside negotiations, not a finding that forecasts are inflated in order to sell loans. The purpose the title names is exactly what the entry's own last paragraph concedes is missing.

settled_by.what_it_is: IEO evaluation report, Growth and Adjustment in IMF-Supported Programs, executive summary
settled_by.what_it_establishes: The Fund's own evaluation office finds growth outcomes "consistently fell short of program projections", blames fiscal-multiplier modelling errors, and says "political economy factors in program negotiations also played a significant role" in ambitious projections. Optimism is documented; selling loans as its purpose is not.

forecasts-inflated-to-sell-loans.still_open: Whether forecasts are raised deliberately, and whether the aim is to get a larger loan approved rather than to reach agreement on a programme. Nobody has compared draft against final appraisal forecasts across a lender's portfolio, which is what the entry itself says is missing.
forecasts-inflated-to-sell-loans.narrower_title: Loan and programme forecasts come out consistently too optimistic

rescues-that-rescue-banks.title_asserts: Big rescue loans are built to repay the borrowing country's private creditors rather than to help the country.
rescues-that-rescue-banks.why: Where the Greek money went is counted and published: under 5 per cent of EUR 215.9 billion reached the budget, with the rest going to old debt, interest and bank recapitalisation. What is documented is that outcome in one programme, plus objections recorded in the IMF's own board room at the time. That rescues are designed this way as a rule is not established, and the entry's third paragraph concedes that who held the bonds at the moment of a rescue is rarely published.

settled_by.what_it_is: ESMT Berlin white paper WP-16-02, Where did the Greek bailout money go? (Rocholl and Stahmer), draft version
settled_by.what_it_establishes: Of EUR 215.9 billion disbursed in the first two programmes, "only EUR 9.7 billion or less than 5%" went to the Greek fiscal budget; EUR 139.2 billion (over 64 per cent) repaid debt and interest and EUR 37.3 billion (17 per cent) recapitalised Greek banks. The same paper puts the root cause of the crisis on Greek budget management, which the entry reports.

rescues-that-rescue-banks.still_open: Whether rescue packages are shaped to get particular creditors out whole, in Greece or anywhere else. Mexico 1995 rests on who held the tesobonos, which has never been published; the board minutes record directors' concerns, not a finding about design.
rescues-that-rescue-banks.narrower_title: Greece's rescue loans went almost entirely to its creditors and its banks

secret-loans-banks-traders.title_asserts: International banks and commodity traders arrange sovereign loans that are kept hidden from the public.
secret-loans-banks-traders.why: This is more than the Mozambique episode. A UK regulator's final notice sets out how the bank arranged the loans and left the IMF uninformed while the first loan's purpose "was still not public knowledge", and the World Bank's own paper lists hidden debt as a recurring problem naming Congo's undisclosed oil-trader prefinancing, Togo's prefinanced debt and Mozambique's undisclosed guarantees. Three sovereigns, two kinds of arranger, in the lenders' own documents, is a practice rather than an anecdote.

settled_by.what_it_is: FCA Final Notice to Credit Suisse International, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) and Credit Suisse AG
settled_by.what_it_establishes: A GBP 147,190,200 penalty. The regulator finds Credit Suisse accepted a general representation of IMF compliance "rather than undertake to inform the IMF of the loans in question", records that the first loan's purpose "was still not public knowledge" in 2014, and that three employees took about $53 million in kick-backs.

settled_by.what_it_is: World Bank, Debt Vulnerabilities in IDA Countries, Box 3 "Hidden Debt"
settled_by.what_it_establishes: The Bank's own paper states there have been "several recent cases of hidden debt among IDA countries": Republic of Congo oil-trader prefinancing contracts undisclosed to the debt management office for over two years, Togo's prefinanced debt missing from official statistics, and Mozambique's 2013 and 2014 guarantees "not disclosed to the debt management staff and the public".

settled_by.what_it_is: Chad: Joint World Bank-IMF Debt Sustainability Analysis, 2018 update
settled_by.what_it_establishes: Chad's commercial debt, "virtually non-existent in 2008", had risen to almost half of external debt, "mostly to Glencore", whose loan is put at about 98 per cent of the commercial debt stock in 2017. It documents the scale of trader lending to a government, though not that Chad's own deals were concealed.

secret-loans-banks-traders.still_open: Whether arranging hidden loans is ordinary business for these banks and traders rather than a set of exposed cases, and how large the unreported total is. No creditor-side comparison for Western banks and traders exists of the kind AidData made for Chinese lenders.
secret-loans-banks-traders.left_over_after_the_duplicate: Not a duplicate, but it overlaps two documented patterns: china-loan-secrecy-collateral already covers Chinese contract secrecy and the underreporting the entry's third paragraph uses, and who-owns-the-debt already carries Mozambique's $2 billion through special companies and the 2024 English High Court bribery finding. The banks-and-traders core (Credit Suisse, Glencore, Trafigura) is not on the page.

poor-countries-take-the-poison.title_asserts: Poor countries are picked out to receive rich countries' toxic waste.
poor-countries-take-the-poison.why: That hazardous waste moves from rich to poor countries, and that governments treat this as a hazard of being poor, is in the treaty the trade produced. The selection the title asserts, countries chosen because harming people there is cheaper, rests on the 1991 memo, which was a memo rather than a decision and which both the man who signed it and the man who wrote it say was sarcasm. Probo Koala and Koko are proven episodes, not proof of the selection rule.

settled_by.what_it_is: Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes, convention text with the Decision III/1 amendment
settled_by.what_it_establishes: The parties record "the increasing desire for the prohibition of transboundary movements of hazardous wastes" to other states, "especially developing countries", and the added paragraph recognises that such movements, "especially to developing countries", carry a high risk of unsound management. The direction of the trade is on the intergovernmental record.

poor-countries-take-the-poison.still_open: Whether destinations are chosen on the cost of harm. No one has matched Basel national export reports against destination wages and treatment capacity, which is the comparison the entry itself names.
poor-countries-take-the-poison.narrower_title: Rich countries' hazardous waste ends up in poor countries

loans-cut-off-to-topple-governments.title_asserts: Lending is cut off through the institutions the West controls in order to bring down governments it dislikes.
loans-cut-off-to-topple-governments.why: The Senate's own investigation establishes the first half: a 1970 policy decision that the United States would use its position in the international financial institutions to dry up new multilateral credit to Chile, with IDB lending falling from $46 million in 1970 to $2 million in 1972, and the committee concluding the actions were political rather than technical. Nixon then announced the instrument in general terms in 1972. What is not established across the three cases is the purpose the title names: in Nicaragua and Haiti the record shows pressure and withheld money, not a documented aim of removing the government.

settled_by.what_it_is: Covert Action in Chile 1963-1973, staff report of the US Senate Select Committee to Study Governmental Operations with Respect to Intelligence Activities
settled_by.what_it_establishes: NSDM 93 of November 1970 provided that the US "would use its predominant position in international financial institutions to dry up the flow of new multilateral credit"; Helms's notes of the 15 September 1970 meeting with Nixon contain "Make the economy scream"; IDB loans fell from $46 million in 1970 to $2 million in 1972, the US holding 40 per cent of IDB votes; the committee finds policy "driven more by political opposition to an Allende regime than by purely technical judgments". Its lending table shows no IBRD disbursements for 1971-73 and $13.5 million in 1974.

loans-cut-off-to-topple-governments.still_open: Whether the aim was to bring governments down rather than to force policy change, in Nicaragua and Haiti above all. US Treasury instructions to its executive directors are largely unreleased, and nobody has counted how often approved or pending loans stalled after disfavoured election results.
loans-cut-off-to-topple-governments.narrower_title: The United States uses its votes at the lending banks to block loans to governments it opposes

documents_i_opened.what_it_is: Church Committee staff report on Chile, 4.2 MB PDF, economic-pressure chapter and lending tables read

aid-traded-for-arms-sales.title_asserts: Donors spend aid money to win arms contracts for their own companies.
aid-traded-for-arms-sales.why: The 1994 judgment settles something narrower than the title: that the Pergau grant fell outside the Overseas Development and Co-operation Act 1980 because the project could not be justified as development. The Foreign Secretary accepted it, dropped an appeal, moved Pergau and three other aid-and-trade projects off the aid vote, and told the Commons that ODA activities were "not in general vulnerable" to the same challenge. The arms link is a separate question the court did not decide: the Commons record shows the Foreign Affairs Committee rejecting Lord Younger's view that the March 1988 protocol did not link aid to arms, while ministers insisted at the despatch box that there is no link between aid and defence sales. Tanzania ended in a plea to an accounting offence, so the bribery allegations were never tried.

settled_by.what_it_is: Statement by the Foreign Secretary, Douglas Hurd, on the Pergau dam (HC Deb 13 December 1994 vol 251 cc773-86)
settled_by.what_it_establishes: The government accepted the divisional court's judgment and decided "not to appeal"; Pergau's outstanding commitments and three further aid-and-trade projects (Ankara metro, an Indonesian television studio, the Botswana flight information region) were moved to funds voted outside the 1980 Act. It settles the unlawfulness of the aid, and says nothing about arms.

settled_by.what_it_is: Commons debate on the Pergau dam (HC Deb 25 January 1995 vol 253 cc274-94)
settled_by.what_it_establishes: Members record that Lord Younger told the Select Committee the protocol he signed on 23 March 1988 "did not link aid with arms expenditure" and that "the Foreign Office and the Government disagreed with that view, as did the Select Committee in its report"; a minister replies that "there is no link between our aid programme and defence sales, and there never has been". The linkage is contested on the official record, in one episode.

aid-traded-for-arms-sales.still_open: Whether aid budgets are bent to win arms and equipment sales as a practice. No donor-by-donor count exists of large aid packages coinciding with arms sales, and in Tanzania the money's destination after the $12 million paid to a marketing adviser was never established.
aid-traded-for-arms-sales.narrower_title: Britain's aid for the Pergau dam was ruled unlawful, and the aid-for-arms link stayed contested

pension-funds-buy-up-farmland.title_asserts: Pension funds and university endowments are the money behind land grabs.
pension-funds-buy-up-farmland.why: The pieces are sourced and the join is not. That the funds hold large farmland in the Cerrado comes from campaign and research groups, GRAIN, Rede Social and Chain Reaction Research, rather than from an official finding; the Incra report that the entry itself calls preliminary is disputed by TIAA; and a frozen deed with a reopened inquiry is a step in a case, not a ruling. What is unresolved is exactly what suspected is for: whether the land was taken unlawfully and whether the funds' money is what took it.
pension-funds-buy-up-farmland.still_open: Whether the holdings rest on illegally claimed public land, and whether the funds knew. No farm-level list of pension fund and endowment farmland is published, so the ownership itself is only as good as the research groups' tracing; the Brazilian proceedings had not concluded.

bondholders-block-debt-relief.title_asserts: Large investment funds refuse debt relief to poor countries and make money from the crisis.
bondholders-block-debt-relief.why: The documented core is already on the page. who-owns-the-debt carries Zambia's missed $42.5 million payment, BlackRock as the largest known holder with $220 million, the $165 million purchase estimate and the 110 per cent profit figure, and the statement that all of Zambia's private lenders except Intesa Sanpaolo refused the September 2020 suspension request. paris-club-versus-china carries the Zambia restructuring and the $6.8 billion held by private creditors.
bondholders-block-debt-relief.still_open: What each fund paid, what it was finally paid, and what it argued in the negotiations. The bondholder committees' records are private.
bondholders-block-debt-relief.left_over_after_the_duplicate: Two things the existing patterns do not carry: the World Bank's own DSSI record ($12.9 billion suspended from May 2020 to December 2021, only one private creditor taking part, and no payments to private lenders suspended in 2020) and the Debt Justice estimate of $20 billion to $30 billion of profit on the bonds of Ethiopia, Ghana, Sri Lanka, Suriname and Zambia. If the entry is kept it should be rebuilt on the scheme-wide record rather than on Zambia, since Zambia is where the overlap sits.

ratings-that-punish-relief.title_asserts: The credit rating agencies downgrade poor countries for asking for debt relief.
ratings-that-punish-relief.why: The African Union's own peer review body records that the key driver of Fitch's two-notch cut on Ethiopia was the government's announcement that it would use the G20 Common Framework, and the UN Development Programme's 2023 brief recommends that a relief appeal "should not lead to rating downgrades", which is a recommendation written because it does. The same thing happened to more than one country: Moody's placed Ethiopia, Cameroon, Senegal and Cote d'Ivoire on review in July 2020 after they joined the suspension scheme. The agencies' stated reasoning is the record here, so this is not an allegation.

settled_by.what_it_is: Statement of the African Peer Review Mechanism, a specialised entity of the African Union, on Fitch's downgrade of Ethiopia
settled_by.what_it_establishes: "The key driver of Ethiopia's rating downgrade is the announcement by the government" that it would use the Common Framework; the cut was two notches, B to CCC, on 9 February 2021, while Moody's and S&P still had the country at B2 and B.

settled_by.what_it_is: UNDP policy brief, Lowering the Costs of Development Finance in Africa
settled_by.what_it_establishes: Puts the cost of rating "idiosyncrasies" at $74.5 billion in excess interest and foregone funding, nearly 12 per cent more than Africa's net ODA in 2020, and recommends that a country's appeal for relief "should not lead to rating downgrades".

settled_by.what_it_is: News report (AFP, following a Financial Times story) on Moody's action against four African countries after they joined the DSSI
settled_by.what_it_establishes: Moody's put Ethiopia, Cameroon, Senegal and Cote d'Ivoire (and Pakistan) up for review "following their decision to join" the scheme, its concern being that suspension could hurt private creditors. This is a press account, not the agency's own notice.

ratings-that-punish-relief.still_open: The wider claims the story makes but the title does not: that poor and African countries are rated more harshly than their figures justify, and that the agencies act to protect the private creditors who pay them. UNDP says the costs may come from thin data and subjective methods rather than conscious bias, rating committee notes are unpublished, and the mortgage-ratings settlements ended with no admission of breaking the law.

companies-behind-coups.title_asserts: Foreign companies are the force behind the overthrow of governments that threaten their investments.
companies-behind-coups.why: The title asserts company authorship, and the declassified record documents something next to it: governments were overthrown after they took foreign companies' assets, and the companies' own governments pressed their claims beforehand. The State Department's published record has Washington telling Guatemala in March 1953 that the compensation offered for 234,000 acres of United Fruit land was inadequate under international law. The entry's own first paragraph concedes that some historians find no proof United Fruit organised the coup, and in Chile the ITT offer was refused. Read as a claim about the twentieth century it is still company influence rather than company direction; read as the continuing practice the story asserts, nothing supports it.

settled_by.what_it_is: Foreign Relations of the United States 1952-1954, volume IV, Editorial Note 420, US State Department Office of the Historian
settled_by.date: note published 1983; events February to August 1953
settled_by.what_it_establishes: Arbenz signed the expropriation of about 234,000 acres of United Fruit land on 26 February 1953, with government bonds as compensation; the United States told Guatemala in an aide-memoire that deferred payment in agrarian bonds was not "prompt and effective compensation" and that the amount was inadequate in international law. It documents the US government acting on the company's claim, not the company directing the coup.

companies-behind-coups.still_open: Whether the companies drove these overthrows rather than benefiting from them and lobbying for them, and whether anything of the kind continues. The entry's own fourth paragraph says records on company involvement after the 1970s are largely closed.
companies-behind-coups.narrower_title: Governments that took foreign companies' assets were overthrown with their home governments' help
